chunks.heading: Super Horse Racing
chunks.bodyHtml: My 1992 high-school GW-BASIC work culminated in Super Horse Racing, my final class project and the first game I ever wrote. The surviving collection also includes a Hong Kong ID validator, a base converter, dice and drawing programs, music, and an unfinished sequel with save/load support.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Source
chunks.heading: Line Numbers, Graphics & Sound
chunks.bodyHtml: The programs use the language exactly as I learned it: numbered statements, GOTO and GOSUB control flow, keyboard input, random numbers, screen graphics, PLAY music, and data files. Each small assignment became another piece of the larger racing game.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / Runner
chunks.heading: The Original Programs, Running Again
chunks.bodyHtml: No port and no rewrite: the preserved .BAS files run with the original GW-BASIC interpreter inside browser-hosted DOS. The showcase can display each recovered source listing, then launch the program through DOSBox and js-dos with its original support files.

chunks.heading: Appleby College Library System
chunks.bodyHtml: My 1994 Grade 13 Computer Science final project was a menu-driven library system written in dBASE III+. It signed books in and out, maintained student and book records, calculated overdue items, printed reports, and included configuration and context-sensitive help screens.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Data
chunks.heading: Menus, Forms & Persistent Records
chunks.bodyHtml: The project joined dozens of .PRG modules to persistent .DBF tables. Data-entry forms, record editing, searches, deletion, reports, error handling, and keyboard-driven menus made it a complete DOS application rather than a collection of isolated database commands.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / Runner
chunks.heading: The Original Project, Running Again
chunks.bodyHtml: The preserved 1994 source, database files, help system, and dBASE runtime now run together inside browser-hosted DOS. The showcase launches Appleby College Library System 2.01r through DOSBox and js-dos and also exposes the original program modules for inspection.

chunks.heading: English Word Collector
chunks.bodyHtml: A summer-vacation exercise I built in 1995 while learning C++, English Word Collector 1.5B is a menu-driven vocabulary database. It can enter, edit, delete, search, list, and print word records containing a date, part of speech, and notes; it also includes a quiz/test, a learning game, save/load, help, and about screens.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Design
chunks.heading: Linked Lists, Sorting & Data-Driven Menus
chunks.bodyHtml: The program keeps records in doubly linked lists sorted both alphabetically and by date, then saves them to TEST.DAT. Its DOS text interface is driven by a binary MENU.INI layout, supported by a separate menu editor and reusable routines for bordered windows, buttons, status lines, dialogs, and listings.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / Runner
chunks.heading: The Original Exercises, Running Again
chunks.bodyHtml: The original Turbo C++ executables now run with their preserved menu and vocabulary data inside browser-hosted DOS. The showcase launches the completed word collector and the smaller exercises I built along the way—box drawing, buttons, animated logos, the menu engine, and the quit dialog—and exposes their original source files.

chunks.heading: Appleby Marking System
chunks.bodyHtml: A three-program Win16 school marks-management suite I wrote in C++ in 1995–96. Manager maintained teachers, classes, students and faculties; Organizer edited class mark tables; Spectator provided read-only views and reports.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Specialty
chunks.heading: MDI Windows and Persistent Records
chunks.bodyHtml: The suite joined a Windows 3.1 multiple-document interface, menus and dialogs to a compact binary database. It was a leap from text-mode tools into event-driven GUI programming: window messages, shared runtime libraries, resources and state that had to survive between sessions.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / Restoration
chunks.heading: The Original Binaries, Running Again
chunks.bodyHtml: No rewrite and no recompile: the original 1996 executables now boot inside a browser-hosted COMPAQ DeskPro 386. I decoded the program's own SAMPLE.AMS backup to restore its teachers, classes and students, then packaged everything on bootable DOS disks for PCjs.

chunks.heading: Macross Tetris
chunks.bodyHtml: My first substantial Java program was Macross Tetris, a two-player applet I wrote in 1996. Two independent playfields run side by side with separate controls, adjustable levels, next-piece and statistics displays, optional matching piece sequences, attack lines, scoring, and a shared high-score table.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Preservation
chunks.heading: Source, Bytecode, Artwork & Upload Logs
chunks.bodyHtml: The original Java source survives with its compiled .class files, Macross artwork, MIDI music, archive, applet page, and 1997 FTP transfer logs. The code preserves its AWT interface, game threads, piece logic, and calls to the long-retired Waterloo score service.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / Restoration
chunks.heading: The Original Applet, Running Again
chunks.bodyHtml: No JavaScript game rewrite and no recompile: the original mactetris.class now runs unchanged through the pinned CheerpJ 4.3 browser JVM. CheerpJ supplies the Java runtime, AWT, threads, and class loading that modern browsers no longer provide through plug-ins.

chunks.heading: Operation Minmay
chunks.bodyHtml: I wrote Operation Minmay for Netscape in 1997. The side-scrolling shooter lets the player choose Roy, Hikaru, Max, or Millia and pilot the matching Valkyrie through eight enemy waves, survive battle pods and incoming fire, defeat the boss, and rescue Minmay before her concert.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Preservation
chunks.heading: JavaScript 1.2, Layers & Original Artwork
chunks.bodyHtml: The original game is preserved with its Netscape and Internet Explorer pages and hand-built artwork. Its Dynamic HTML engine moved dozens of absolutely positioned <layer> objects with timers, keyboard events, collision checks, enemy formations, projectiles, explosions, energy, and scoring.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / Compatibility
chunks.heading: From Netscape Layers to Canvas
chunks.bodyHtml: Modern browsers removed Netscape's layer API, so the compatibility edition recreates the original mission and control flow with Canvas 2D, DOM events, and requestAnimationFrame. The pilots, artwork, enemy waves, boss battle, controls, and ending remain, while the untouched original page stays available as historical source.

chunks.heading: A 68000 Calculator on Real I/O
chunks.bodyHtml: My 1997 E&CE 222 labs targeted a Motorola 68000 training board and its TUTOR monitor. The integrated program presents a serial menu, scans a 4×4 parallel keypad, and runs a signed four-function calculator through hand-written input, output, arithmetic, and conversion routines.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Preservation
chunks.heading: Source, Opcodes & Hardware Addresses
chunks.bodyHtml: The original .ASM files survive beside zero-error assembler listings containing addresses and emitted opcodes. The code talks directly to the ACIA at $010040/$010042 and a 6821-style parallel interface at $010001–$010013—registers, polling loops, debounce delays, and no operating system.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / Workbench
chunks.heading: Run It One Instruction at a Time
chunks.bodyHtml: The browser workbench recreates the original control flow at source level: set breakpoints on preserved lines, single-step across modules, use the keypad, and observe D0–D7, A0–A7, PC, stack, and calculator state. Reconstructed link addresses are identified honestly because the final 1997 linked image did not survive.

chunks.heading: Describing Silicon Before It Exists
chunks.bodyHtml: VHDL — IEEE 1076, 1987 — is one of two languages used to design every digital chip on Earth. The mind-flip: it's not a program that runs — it's a description of a circuit that exists. Write c <= a and b; and you've specified a physical AND gate etched into silicon.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Specialty
chunks.heading: Concurrency, Signals & Simulation
chunks.bodyHtml: Everything in VHDL happens in parallel — because that's how hardware works. You simulate before fabrication because you can't patch silicon. A bug costs millions and months.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / My Take
chunks.heading: My Day Job, My Native Layer
chunks.bodyHtml: VHDL is where my journey converges. Everything above is built on hardware described in languages like this. When a bug spans firmware, OS, and silicon, I chase it from RTL waveform up to the JS console and back. Fifty years in, the loop is closed: the kid who typed GOTO 10 now designs the gates that fetch it.

chunks.heading: Embeddable Glue
chunks.bodyHtml: Tcl — the Tool Command Language — was created by John Ousterhout at Berkeley as a tiny, embeddable scripting engine. Pair it with Tk, its GUI toolkit, and you could build a cross-platform windowed app in a dozen lines. EDA vendors loved it — the command consoles inside virtually every chip-design tool speak Tcl.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Specialty
chunks.heading: The Language Inside the Tools
chunks.bodyHtml: Tcl's specialty is being hosted. "Everything is a command, everything is a string." Minimalist enough to drive a tool, flexible enough to script complex flows. Tk proved GUIs didn't require C++ and a week of boilerplate.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / My Take
chunks.heading: Driving the EDA Engines
chunks.bodyHtml: Tcl is the common tongue of chip design. Whether I'm scripting synthesis or automating place-and-route, the console is almost always Tcl. It taught me that a powerful tool is really a programmable tool — the best engineers don't click buttons, they script the engine. Every tapeout I've shipped has Tcl threading through its spine.

chunks.heading: The Pipe & the Filter
chunks.bodyHtml: The Unix shell — sh, csh, and especially tcsh on Berkeley Unix — is the original "glue language." Chain tiny tools with |: grep, sed, awk, sort. Composability as a philosophy. tcsh added filename completion, history editing, and job control.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Specialty
chunks.heading: Composable Automation
chunks.bodyHtml: The shell's superpower is orthogonal composition: every tool reads stdin and writes stdout, so any pipeline just works. It is the duct tape that has held engineering together for fifty years.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / My Take
chunks.heading: Automation as a Reflex
chunks.bodyHtml: The shell is where I learned that if you do it twice, script it. Every chip project I run is stitched together by tcsh and Make — nightly regressions, coverage merges, log scraping. The AI chips I help build are born inside shell scripts that kick off a thousand simulations and report back in green PASS.

chunks.heading: The Pioneer of Random Verification
chunks.bodyHtml: The e language, created by Yoav Hollander at Verisity (later Cadence), was the original constrained-random verification language — predating SystemVerilog/UVM by years. Its Aspect-Oriented features let engineers inject checks anywhere without touching the original code.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Specialty
chunks.heading: Aspects & Temporal Checking
chunks.bodyHtml: e's specialties are Aspect-Oriented Programming — weave new behavior into existing code without modifying it — and powerful temporal assertions that check sequences over time. It made verification a first-class engineering discipline.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / My Take
chunks.heading: Learning to Trust Randomness
chunks.bodyHtml: e taught me a counterintuitive truth: the best tester is one that surprises you. Hand-written tests find the bugs you imagined; random verification finds the ones you didn't. That philosophy — define the rules, then let the machine explore — is exactly how I think about AI today.

chunks.heading: One Language, Two Jobs
chunks.bodyHtml: SystemVerilog (IEEE 1800) merged Verilog's design syntax with a powerful OOP verification layer. Then UVM made it possible to build reusable, randomized test environments for the most complex chips ever built. It is the industry standard for taping out modern silicon.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Specialty
chunks.heading: Constrained-Random Verification
chunks.bodyHtml: SystemVerilog's superpower is constrained random testing: describe the legal input space, and the solver blasts millions of edge-case scenarios at your design, hunting bugs no human would think to write. Combined with functional coverage, it turns "did we test enough?" into a measurable number.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / My Take
chunks.heading: Proving the Chip Before It's Real
chunks.bodyHtml: SystemVerilog + UVM is how I sleep at night before a tapeout. On an AI accelerator, you can't test every MAC by hand — you let the randomized environment find the one-in-a-billion collision. Verification is harder than design, and coverage is a moral contract with the silicon.

chunks.heading: Optimized for Joy
chunks.bodyHtml: Yukihiro "Matz" Matsumoto designed Ruby with one goal: programmer happiness. Everything is an object. Blocks, closures, and a syntax that reads almost like English. When Rails arrived in 2004, Ruby became the fastest way to ship a web app, and a generation of startups was born on it.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Specialty
chunks.heading: Expressiveness & DSLs
chunks.bodyHtml: Ruby's specialty is malleability — you can bend its syntax into a domain-specific language. Rails reads like declarative poetry: has_many :comments. It prioritized developer flow over machine speed, a radical idea at the time.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / My Take
chunks.heading: The Value of Beauty
chunks.bodyHtml: Ruby taught me that code can be beautiful, and beauty matters. After years of terse C and rigid Java, Ruby's expressiveness felt like oxygen. It trained me to value readability and developer experience — principles I now apply to RTL testbenches and build scripts. Elegance is a form of engineering discipline, not vanity.

chunks.heading: Batteries Included
chunks.bodyHtml: Python, named after Monty Python, was built to be readable above all. NumPy, Pandas, and PyTorch made it the lingua franca of AI. Today, every neural network training run on Earth begins with import torch.

chunks.label: ▸ 02 / Specialty
chunks.heading: The Universal Glue
chunks.bodyHtml: Python's specialty is breadth: it wraps C/C++/Fortran libraries, scripts EDA flows, runs web servers, and trains trillion-parameter models. Readable enough for a beginner, powerful enough to run the world's AI.

chunks.label: ▸ 03 / My Take
chunks.heading: The Bridge to AI Silicon
chunks.bodyHtml: Python is the bridge between my two worlds. The AI models that my chips accelerate are defined and trained in Python; the scripts that verify those same chips are Python too. The engineer who speaks both PyTorch and RTL is the one who can actually ship the silicon that powers it. Python closed that loop for me.
